headlines.title: Woman struck, killed while riding electric scooter in San Francisco identified
headlines.description: A woman who was struck and killed Friday while riding an electric scooter on Market Street was identified by the San Francisco Medical Examiner’s Office. Yebin Kim, a 32-year-old woman from San Francisco, was identified as the victim of the collision. On Friday at 8:18 a.m., San Francisco police responded to reports of a vehicle collision at Powell and Market streets. At the scene, officers found Kim in the street and provided first aid until medical personnel arrived. She was pronounced dead on scene. Police said the collision was between a standup electric scooter and a commercial vehicle. The driver of the vehicle was located and cooperated with the investigation. The SFPD Traffic Collision Investigation Unit is conducting the investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact SFPD at 415-575-4444 or text a tip to TIP411.

headlines.title: FAA announces plans to partially roll back SFO restrictions, allow more landings
headlines.description: Restrictions placed on operating procedures at San Francisco International Airport will be revised by the Federal Aviation Administration on Wednesday, potentially increasing the number of aircraft that can be processed at one of the busiest airports in the country. Officials at the FAA and at SFO confirmed a previous ban on parallel approaches will be “slightly revised” to now included staggered arrivals, with the goal to maximize the use of the airport’s existing landing strips after losing the usage of others to planned maintenance. The new rules will allow, weather permitting, up to 42 aircrafts per hour, six more than before the change, but still less than what the airport maintained with parallel landings. It comes at a time when SFO is operating with reduced capacity because of ongoing maintenance to its runways, with one currently being used as a taxiway while the others alternating between landings and takeoffs. Doug Yakel, the airport’s spokesperson, confirmed the new staggered arrivals procedure is starting Wednesday. Airplanes will be arriving at staggered times, alternating which runway they use, which will help increase the number of landings and takeoffs in a limited timeframe. “While this will not fully restore the arrival rate we had when true side-by-side landings were permitted, this is nonetheless a step in the right direction,” said Yakel. SFO has two sets of parallel runways, with the center lines of each runway pair 750 feet from one another. According to the FAA, airports must ensure aircraft have a few thousand feet of horizontal separation for simultaneous operations. More steps are required depending on closeness, but no other airport in the U.S. shares the same frequency and distance of runways as SFO. Prior to March 30, SFO operated for decades under an FAA-approved waiver. The “double landings” saw aircraft land close to one another, with some passengers being able to see others on the adjacent plane. Pilots were instructed to carefully follow visual flight rules to maintain separation by watching neighboring airplanes and responding appropriately without air traffic control input. The practice became an iconic part of landing at SFO. United Airlines, who is the largest single carrier at SFO, praised the move to increase the number of aircraft movements. The Chicago-based airline said it “appreciated the FAA’s decision” and that the company had “been working closely with them to increase landing rates at SFO that safely make the best use of the airport’s capacity.” While the FAA has stated aircraft accidents did not prompt the banning of the parallel approaches, officials say safety is paramount at busy airports like SFO. While the airport is now allowed to clear up to 40 aircraft per hour for landings, it may increase to 42 by the end of the month. As of Wednesday afternoon, SFO remains capped at 36 arrivals an hour as a ground delay program is in place because of low visibility. Delays for flights from across the country and Canada are estimated to reach an hour.
headlines.source: Andres Jimenez Larios | Bay City News

headlines.title: Food pantry in Hayward to close after more than 50 years of service
headlines.description: A food pantry in Hayward that’s been serving the community for over 50 years will shut down at the end of the week. South Hayward Parish’s last day of food distribution will be Friday, First Presbyterian Church of Hayward announced. The site’s emergency shelter and resource center for unhoused residents will stay open. “We have worked and prayed to discern how to best steward our resources and live our mission to meet community needs, and it has become clear that operating both a food pantry and shelter on the same campus is no longer sustainable,” FirstPres Hayward said in a statement on its website. “Therefore, we have made the difficult decision to discontinue food pantry operations so we can focus fully on serving our unhoused neighbors.” The emergency shelter provides year-round access for 25 unhoused residents, and the daytime resource centers offers case management, meals, showers, laundry, and housing and healthcare connections, according to FirstPres Hayward. “While the number of individuals we house can’t increase because of space restrictions, the programs we provide can become more robust, ensuring more guests are connected to housing more quickly, and therefore making a greater impact on the experience of homelessness in South Hayward,” FirstPres Hayward said in a statement. Alternative food distribution sites in the area can be found below.

headlines.title: 1 dead, 1 hurt in Richmond stabbing
headlines.description: One person died and another was injured in a stabbing in Richmond, police said Wednesday. Richmond police said they received a report at about 11:18 p.m. Tuesday of a stabbing in the 1700 block of Wood Place. Responding officers and medical personnel found two victims suffering from stab wounds, according to police. Both victims were transported to the hospital to be treated, but one victim did not survive. The other victim was listed in stable condition and is expected to survive. Homicide unit detectives responded to the stabbing scene and took over the investigation. Police did not immediately release any information about a suspect. Investigators believe the stabbing was an isolated incident, police said, adding that there was no active threat to the community. An investigation is underway. Anyone with information is asked to call the Richmond Police Department at 510-233-1214.

headlines.title: Bay Area science centers to host eclipse, meteor shower events
headlines.description: Bay Area science institutions will host several events Wednesday for people interested in astronomy, including watch parties for a total solar eclipse and the Perseid meteor shower. The Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland will host a NASA livestream of the total solar eclipse beginning at 10 a.m., with Iceland’s eclipse occurring around 10:45 a.m. A Perseid meteor shower watch party is scheduled for 11 p.m. at the center at 10000 Skyline Blvd. The California Academy of Sciences and SETI Institute will host a total solar eclipse event at 10:30 a.m. featuring livestreams from Iceland and northern Spain, along with a live performance by the International Space Orchestra. The event will be held at 55 Music Concourse Drive in San Francisco. The Exploratorium will also host an eclipse watch party at 10:30 a.m. with a live telescope broadcast from Spain, where totality is expected at 11:28 a.m. The event will be at Pier 15 on the Embarcadero, San Francisco. headlines.title: Big Sur Timber Fire nears 3,800 acres as nonprofit launches fundraiser
headlines.description: The Timber Fire burning in the Big Sur area of Monterey County continued to grow on Wednesday, scorching nearly 3,800 acres by midday. The fire remained stubbornly 5% contained at that time. Up to 640 residents were under evacuation orders and another roughly 350 were under evacuation warnings, according to Monterey County’s Department of Emergency Management. An overnight shelter for those under evacuation orders was established at Carmel Middle School. Three people stayed overnight Tuesday, according to the county. The middle school is also serving as a temporary evacuation point for anyone under evacuation warnings who needs information or support. Cal Fire Battalion Chief Josh Silveira said during a virtual media briefing on the fire Wednesday that humidity had slightly increased, which was favorable for fighting the flames. “But we can’t change topography, so, that’s going to be a challenge no matter what,” Silveira said. State Highway 1 was closed for a 10-mile stretch in the area southeast of Loma Vista to facilitate firefighting operations. Silveira acknowledged the difficulty of getting through the area for residents who depend on the highway for movement in the forested coastal area. “We don’t take those road closures lightly,” he said. The nonprofit organization Community Foundation for Monterey County began a fundraiser for residents impacted by the fire. There were over 900 firefighters and a range of airborne equipment from throughout the state assigned to the fire. Over 500 structures were threatened as of Wednesday, including several iconic Big Sur properties known for high-end lodging and dining, including Nepenthe, Alila Ventana Big Sur, The Sur House, and Sierra Mar.

headlines.title: Lithium-ion battery fires a growing problem for Bay Area recycling centers
headlines.description: Joe La Mariana will never forget the night: Sept. 7, 2016. It was 8 p.m., and La Mariana was working out on his exercycle. Then he got the phone call. “It was a four-alarm fire,” said La Mariana, the executive director of RethinkWaste, a recycling and disposal agency that serves the San Francisco Peninsula. “Our materials recovery facility [MRF] — the place where mixed materials from recycling bins are sorted and prepared for sale — was burning. I went down there immediately. It took a hundred firefighters to get it under control, and I didn’t get home until 4 a.m.” There were multiple negative ramifications from the blaze, said La Mariana. “Our MRF was out of commission for four months, the recyclable materials we typically process had to be sent to other sorting facilities, and we had to lay off 80 employees,” said La Mariana. “Before the fire, our insurance policy cost about $180,000 a year. That jumped to $3.1 million in two years because of the perceived risk.” And what’s driving that growing risk of dangerous, polluting trash fires? Ironically, a technology popularly associated with “green” economics: lithium-ion batteries, the devices that power EVs and store energy for large solar arrays. The advantages of lithium-ion batteries are many: they are light, recharge quickly, and store large amounts of power. But they have one profound downside: if they are ruptured or damaged, they can burst into flames. Worse, the fires aren’t easily extinguished — they are essentially runaway chemical reactions. “You can’t put them out through any of the usual ways,” said La Mariana. “They burn white hot. You have to isolate the actual battery from the waste material and let it burn out.” To mitigate the threat, the agency has installed automatically activated water cannons in their MRFs. “But they just drench the recyclable materials so they can’t burn,” said La Mariana. They don’t actually extinguish the battery fire itself.” Concerns remain high for RethinkWaste since that massive 2016 conflagration; La Mariana said the agency still responds monthly to fires in its MRF. Some are caused by pressurized gas containers — used propane and butane canisters or oxygen tanks that people toss in their blue bins, thinking it’s okay “because they’re metal.” But that lapse in thinking can have catastrophic consequences when the canisters are crushed by a loader or other piece of heavy equipment or crunched up in machinery that compresses and bales recyclable materials. Still, lithium-ion batteries remain the major fire threat — and it’s one that’s growing, said Maurice Quillen, the vice president and general manager at Recology San Francisco, a sister agency of RethinkWaste that has lost recycling trucks to battery fires. “The batteries have been around for a long time, but their use has expanded dramatically in recent years,” said Quillen. “They’re in a vast number of consumer products now — cellphones, cars, scooters, tools, toys, even vapes. And as municipalities have stepped up their recycling efforts, these batteries are increasingly ending up in the waste stream.” That risk isn’t just localized, La Mariana emphasized. Recycling centers bale cardboard, plastics and other materials for overseas sales. Lithium-ion batteries unintentionally packed with recyclables can ignite, threatening the container ships transporting them. “Ship fires [associated with lithium-battery packs] already have occurred, and the threat and concern are growing as more and more of these batteries are produced,” La Mariana said. It might seem obvious that it’s a bad idea to throw a lithium-ion battery in the garbage or recycling bins, said Quillen, but not all consumers are aware of the hazards. And even those that are may be unsure of what to do with the batteries and products containing them. “Often they may not even know the type of battery their device has, or how they can extract it for disposal,” said Quillen. “Smartphones, for example — in most cases, it’s now impossible for the average consumer to remove their batteries. So in exasperation, people just toss the phones in their blue bins. There’s a lot of education that needs to be done.” La Mariana agrees with Quillen that recycling agencies need to ramp up consumer awareness. “We’ve even seen Tesla battery packs thrown in the recycling bins, so we’ve increased our outreach program to meet the challenge,” he said. “If you have batteries — any batteries — to dispose of, put them in zip lock bags and place them on top of the black garbage bin when you set out your containers for collection. The driver will stop and pick them up. Some recycling centers also have special disposal areas for batteries and e-waste.” But regulation also is needed, said Quillen — and on that front, there’s been some progress. Assembly Bill 762, a bill that would phase out single-use disposable vapes and e-cigarettes that incorporate lithium-ion batteries, is currently pending in the state Senate Appropriations Committee. And Senate Bill 501 is before the Assembly Appropriations Committee; it would require greater “producer responsibility” — e.g., manufacturer buyback — for the lithium-ion batteries commonly used in e-bikes, lawn tools and similar mid-sized products. Both bills are expected to pass into law. “We definitely need some stewardship rules on these products,” said Quillen, “and these bills are a good start.”

headlines.title: SF fire commissioners face backlash over removing peer counselors from 911 calls
headlines.description: San Francisco fire commissioners are facing backlash over a recent decision to remove peer counselors from 911 calls. Advocates say the counselors work alongside paramedics to help people experiencing mental health or substance use crises. Opponents of the decision say removing the counselors will make emergency responses less effective. Fire department leaders, however, say the change is needed, citing scheduling challenges and an evolving 911 system. Community members attended Wednesday’s Fire Commission meeting to speak out against the decision.

headlines.title: Jury awards $33 million to twin girls who lost parents in Redwood City crash
headlines.description: A San Mateo County jury found Cesar Morales, Kyle Harrison and Morales’ parents liable in the wrongful death case stemming from the November 2022 crash that killed Greg Ammen and Grace Spiridon. The jury awarded $33 million in economic and non-economic damages on Tuesday to the twin girls whose parents were killed in a high-speed crash on El Camino Real in Redwood City nearly four years ago. The verdict came after a roughly three-week trial stemming from the crash that killed Ammen, 44, and Spiridon, 42, as the family was driving to their San Carlos home with their then-7-year-old daughters. The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 on behalf of the twin girls and alleged that the two drivers’ reckless street racing caused their parents’ deaths. The jury found Morales, who was 17 at the time of the crash, and 23-year-old Harrison liable for the couple’s deaths. Jurors also found Morales’ parents, Arnold Morales and Susana Salto Alvarez, liable for negligent supervision, concluding they allowed their teenage son to drive despite warning signs surrounding his driving history. Redwood City Jun 6, 2024 Redwood City Jan 17, 2025 Redwood City Mar 17, 2025 The girls, now 11, survived the crash and were later adopted by their aunt Liza Spiridon and uncle. Following the verdict Spiridon said, “When the truth prevails, it doesn’t just vindicate — it heals.” She added, “It gives grief somewhere to rest, turns silence into evidence, and hands the people left behind something they can finally stand on: not closure, but clarity.” Evidence in the trial alleged that Morales was traveling over 100 mph before striking the family’s vehicle as it turned left on Finger Avenue on El Camino Real. Harrison was traveling nearby and although his vehicle did not strike the family’s car, the plaintiffs argued that he and Morales were racing and that their actions contributed to the deadly collision. Jurors also heard evidence that Morales had previously received citations for driving more than 100 mph and using a cell phone while driving. His parents testified they did not know about those citations mailed to the home they share with their son. Jurors found Cesar Morales most responsible for the crash, assigning him 60% of the fault. Arnold Morales was assigned 20%, Susana Salto 5%, and Kyle Harrison 15%. Attorney for the plaintiffs, Niall McCarthy, said following the verdict that the case should serve as a warning to parents of teenage drivers. “You cannot ignore warning signs with your teenage children,” McCarthy said. “Parents need to do more than simply provide a car and hope for the best. They need to act when it is apparent their child needs a course correction.” He added, “Here, tragically, two young girls no longer have parents because of the Morales family’s decisions.” The civil verdict comes after separating criminal proceedings against Morales and Harrison. In juvenile court, Morales was found responsible for two felony counts of vehicular manslaughter and street-racing. He spent approximately over two years in juvenile hall. Harrison, who was an adult at the time of the crash, pleaded no contest to two counts of felony vehicular manslaughter and one count of felony street racing. He was sentenced to eight years in state prison. On March 15, 2025, weeks after his sentencing, Harrison was found unresponsive in his cell at the Maple Street Correctional Center in Redwood City and later pronounced dead. The San Mateo County Coroner’s Office determined Harrison died from the toxic effects of methadone, amitriptyline and gabapentin and ruled his death accidental. Harrison’s parents and estate are suing San Mateo County and others over his death in custody, alleging jail and medical personnel were responsible for administering medications that contributed to his fatal overdose. Morales and his parents have also filed a separate civil rights lawsuit against Redwood City, San Mateo County and other government agencies involved in the investigation and prosecution of the 2022 crash. That lawsuit alleges, among other things, that investigators prematurely characterized the crash as street racing and that Morales’ constitutional rights were violated during the investigation and juvenile proceedings. Government defendants have denied wrongdoing and challenged the claims.

headlines.title: Jury selection begins in Meta youth social media addiction trial
headlines.description: Meta faces states including California in an Oakland federal court over allegations that its Facebook and Instagram apps are designed to keep minors hooked. Jury selection began Wednesday morning, according to the court calendar. The trial is scheduled to start Monday morning. Attorneys general from 29 states, including California, allege social media companies illegally collected and used children’s data and designed their platforms to keep young users engaged while misleading the public about their safety. Meta is set to go to trial first, while other companies, including Google and TikTok’s parent company ByteDance, face similar allegations. The broader lawsuits also name Snapchat, YouTube and Alphabet. Advocates say features including infinite scrolling, autoplay, algorithmic recommendations, push notifications and engagement metrics such as “likes” can lead to harmful outcomes for young users, including depression, anxiety, eating disorders, self-harm, suicidal ideation and other mental health issues. The Meta case could serve as a bellwether, potentially shaping how lower courts view future lawsuits involving social media companies.

headlines.title: Pedestrian struck by vehicle in San Jose dies days later
headlines.description: A San Jose pedestrian who was struck by a car earlier this month and then stabilized at a hospital has died, police said. On Aug. 4 just after noon, officers responded to a vehicle versus pedestrian collision in the area of Tully Road and Lucretia Avenue. According to police, a woman driving a Nissan Sentra was going westbound on Tully Road and making a right turn into Lucretia Avenue when she struck a man who was crossing Lucretia in a marked crosswalk. The man was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries but was later stabilized. The woman who struck him remained at the scene and was cooperative. On Sunday, the man succumbed to his injuries and died. His identity has not been released. This was the 14th pedestrian death in San Jose this year, according to the department on Tuesday.

headlines.title: San Mateo County may require permit for businesses using humanoid robots
headlines.description: Will humanoid robots be safe and regulated? That is the question San Mateo County is examining as more businesses consider using humanoid robots. “We see this coming at us now,” San Mateo County Supervisor Ray Mueller said. “And we have an opportunity right now.” Supervisors met Tuesday to discuss a county plan that would require businesses using robots to buy a permit. Money from permit sales would then go to buy extra firefighting equipment needed to put out lithium-ion battery fires. “It’s a real problem for firefighters, both because you need specialized equipment in order to fight that fire, but also because as that fire is occurring, it’s releasing chemicals into the air that are detrimental to their health,” Mueller said. County leaders admit the plan being discussed is early but want to be prepared knowing the robots are on the way.
